one_liner: Breadth-first, find-compatible directory search tool with parallel async I/O; about 3x faster than GNU find on full traversals.
what_it_does: A command-line replacement for find that accepts POSIX, GNU, BSD and macOS find syntax but visits files shallowest-first. It adds extensions such as -exclude, -nohidden, typo suggestions and a static analyzer that warns about expressions whose results are ignored. It is a CLI binary, not a library; integration means calling it in place of find.
how_it_is_fast: Since 3.0 directories are opened and read asynchronously by background worker threads (default: number of CPUs, capped at 8, set with -jN) fed through a lock-free MPMC ring queue (src/ioq.c) that uses unconditional fetch-and-add instead of compare-and-swap. Since 3.1, on Linux with liburing, each worker also drives an io_uring for openat, close and statx, and stat() calls run in parallel on all platforms. Breadth-first order means -quit searches for shallow targets stop before descending into deep unrelated subtrees.
when_to_use: Shell scripts or tools that shell out to find and walk large trees (home directories, monorepos, kernel or Chromium checkouts)
Searches for a file you expect to be near the top of a deep tree, with -print -quit
Queries needing per-file metadata (-size, -newer, -links, colorized output), which benefit from parallel stat
Linux boxes with liburing available, or macOS/BSD where the threaded path still applies
When you need exact find semantics (the author reports no other find passes even the POSIX subset of its test suite)
when_not_to_use: You need a C or C++ library API for directory walking; bfs is only a binary (bftw.c is internal, not a supported library)
You want gitignore-aware, regex-first search with friendly defaults; fd covers that interface (bfs needs -nohidden/-exclude)
Output order must match GNU find's depth-first order exactly, e.g. diffing against existing find output
Machines with very low open-file limits or many concurrent instances; 4.1.1 only recently started respecting system-wide limits
Workloads dominated by -exec of a child process, where traversal speed is not the bottleneck

integration.form: CLI binary (built with ./configure && make; packaged in most Linux distros, Homebrew, MacPorts, FreeBSD, OpenBSD)
integration.dependencies: none required beyond a C compiler, GNU make and Bash; optional libacl, libcap, libselinux, liburing, oniguruma
integration.min_toolchain: C23 by default since 4.1; C17 fallback if the compiler supports common extensions; needs <stdatomic.h> and pthreads
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD, DragonFly BSD, Illumos, Android, WASIX; io_uring path Linux-only with feature probing
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (standalone process; internally multi-threaded, -j1 disables background threads' parallelism)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — accepts find's syntax and passes find's semantics tests, but output order is breadth-first, not depth-first, and -mount follows POSIX 2024 (excludes mount points)

gotchas: Default ./configure is a debug build; benchmark or package with ./configure --enable-release or results will be slower
io_uring is used for openat/close/statx only; reading directory entries (getdents) still goes through readdir in worker threads (ioq.c carries a TODO for io_uring_prep_getdents)

Several long-lived optimizer bugs were fixed recently: 4.0.8 fixed '-user a -or -user b' being rewritten to '-user a' (since 2.0), and 4.1.4 fixed -size units being ignored by the optimizer (since 1.3.3), which could return no results
3.1.2/3.1.3 fixed io_uring feature probing on older 5.x kernels; very old liburing builds were fixed in 4.0.5
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick bfs over al-dente (dent) when you need full find expression compatibility and a mature, packaged tool rather than a narrower listing utility; pick it over fd when the script already speaks find syntax or targets are shallow. For disk-usage totals, diskus, gdu or pdu are more direct.
verified_claims_summary: Per WebSearch snippets of the author's bfs 3.0 blog post (page itself blocked): a full traversal of a ~7.6M-file home directory with -false took bfs 3.0.1 2.416 s vs GNU find 7.021 s (2.9x), bfs 2.6.3 5.307 s (2.2x) and fd 8.209 s; an early-quit search (-name kd-forest.mkv -quit) ran 427.6x faster than find and 248.7 +/- 159.3x faster than fd, a breadth-first-order effect with very high variance. CPU, compiler and flags were not visible in the snippets; the repo's bench/bench.sh (hyperfine -w2 -M20, Linux v6.5, Rust and Chromium 119 corpora) reproduces the setup but publishes no results.
status_note: Actively maintained (4.1.4 released June 29, 2026; CI and coverage), 0BSD-licensed and widely packaged, so it can be installed rather than vendored.
